concepts.name: immersive experience
concepts.definition: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

defining_facts.text: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

concepts.name: head-mounted display
concepts.definition: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

defining_facts.text: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors.
In 1961, engineers at Philco Corporation developed an early head-mounted display (HMD) that could track users' motion but was bulky and uncomfortable to wear.
In 1965, Tom Furness and colleagues at the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base worked on visually coupled systems for pilots that consisted of head-mounted displays (HMDs).
In 1967, Sutherland developed the Sword of Damocles, a head-mounted display (HMD), and was the first to demonstrate an HMD with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

In 1985, Scott Fisher and colleagues at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) developed and launched Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED), the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic head-tracked head-mounted display (HMD) with a wide field of view.

The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.
Although head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be used as input to track head motion, their primary use is as a display device.
A head-mounted display (HMD) is a sophisticated piece of equipment that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components within its package.

A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.
Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.

Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

concepts.name: interaction
concepts.definition: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.

defining_facts.text: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.
Interaction in non-immersive settings, such as augmented reality (AR), is similar to familiar interactions such as touch and gesture.

For immersive virtual reality (VR) or mixed reality (MR) experiences, specialized techniques and setups are used, and suitable interaction techniques should be known and used to design the experience properly and enhance presence.

Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.

In computer graphics, interaction is the manipulation of an image or parts of it by a user using input devices, such as a joystick or devices associated with virtual reality (VR) input, which changes the object's appearance and the screen.

The fundamental problem of computer graphics gives rise to four basic issues: representing objects or parts of an image; synthesizing parts to form complete realistic imagery; allowing users to manipulate images on a screen, which is related to interactive systems; and creating the perception of motion, which is related to animation.

concepts.name: augmented reality system
concepts.definition: The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

defining_facts.text: The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

An augmented reality (AR) system has four characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content such as image, video, or text; the enhancement is registered in 3D so that it appears at its appropriate place rather than randomly and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects; the enhancement is experienced through the user's sensory organs; and the system supports the user's interaction with the digital content in the enhanced environment rather than separately, giving the user the feel of being in reality at all times.

A system is identified as an augmented reality (AR) system by checking the four AR characteristics one by one, and it is an AR system only if all four are satisfied; if at least one characteristic is not satisfied, it is not an AR system.

concepts.name: ray
concepts.definition: The ray view of light describes light as rays, which are trajectories or paths assumed to be traces of the motion of a single hypothetical photon, and it is helpful for explaining how lenses work and the concept of visibility.

defining_facts.text: The ray view of light describes light as rays, which are trajectories or paths assumed to be traces of the motion of a single hypothetical photon, and it is helpful for explaining how lenses work and the concept of visibility.

concepts.name: cone
concepts.definition: The human eye contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, in which rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina and cones are mainly located in the small central region of the retina called the fovea.

defining_facts.text: The human eye contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, in which rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina and cones are mainly located in the small central region of the retina called the fovea.
Multiple rods can share a single optic nerve fiber, which aids sensitivity to lower levels of light, whereas approximately one optic nerve fiber serves each cone, which aids image acuity.

Vision accomplished only with cones is photopic vision, which is more related to direct or central vision, and vision accomplished only with rods is scotopic vision, which is more related to peripheral vision.

Color is perceived only in photopic vision, which is accomplished with cones and gives a sense of color, whereas in scotopic vision weak lights are perceived as a series of grays and color perception is not that good.

concepts.name: degree of freedom
concepts.definition: The concept of degrees of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space.

defining_facts.text: The concept of degrees of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space.

In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.
In a virtual world, motion is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported.

concepts.name: six degrees of freedom
concepts.definition: In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.

concepts.name: object interaction
concepts.definition: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

defining_facts.text: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.

In any virtual experience, object interaction is broadly of two types: selection, which specifies one or more objects from a set of virtual objects in the virtual world, and manipulation, which interacts with a selected object to change its properties; the two types mostly have separate interaction techniques.

concepts.name: navigation
concepts.definition: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

defining_facts.text: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.
The goal of navigation in a virtual world is to move the user from one point to another, which means a change of the user's field of view or viewpoint.
The movement involved in navigation in a virtual world has two parts: the travel part and the wayfinding part.
Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.

never_defined.name: interaction technique
never_defined.definition: The phases of augmented reality (AR) evolution are characterized as follows: the experimental phase involved early experimentation that defined the concepts and showed the types of technology required for AR; the basic research phase involved research into enabling technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices; the tools or applications phase involved developing or exploring early applications and exploratory tasks related to interaction techniques, usability of such applications, and design theory for AR; and the commercial application phase involved widespread AR availability and newer applications appearing in domains such as gaming, medicine, mobile, commerce, and marketing.

never_defined.name: orientation
never_defined.definition: To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.

never_defined.name: controller

never_defined.name: gesture
never_defined.definition: Bend-sensing data gloves are data gloves with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions; their processing unit receives continuous raw data from these bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures, and because their many sensors make any gesture likely to generate a different data stream for unambiguous interpretation, they provide a large degree of freedom that can make interaction more natural than controller-based interaction.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional scene
never_defined.definition: The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves.

never_defined.name: hand gesture

never_defined.name: head position

never_defined.definition: Combining sound with vision or visual effects affects perception of properties of the virtual environment, such as size, volume, material, intensity, and distance, and although looking alone partly gives an idea of those properties, perception of them is reinforced when vision is augmented with auditory effects.

never_defined.name: direction
never_defined.definition: The spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location has three parameters: azimuth, the angle in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the projection of the sound source direction, ranging from -180 degrees to 180 degrees; elevation, the angle between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane, ranging from -90 degrees to 90 degrees; and radius, the distance from the listener's head origin to the source.

never_defined.definition: The overall goal of haptic exploration is to integrate somatosensory signals from in-hand manipulation of an object so that a geometric mental model of the object is learned in terms of properties such as shape, size, weight and hardness.

never_defined.definition: Touch sensation in extended reality (XR) can be provided by engineered devices, and the most popular form is force feedback, typically in the form of vibrations, provided by force feedback devices such as a force feedback mouse, smart gloves, and body suits, which are common in many XR systems, particularly virtual reality (VR) systems.

never_defined.name: one-to-one mapping
never_defined.definition: The virtual hand technique is the simplest and most intuitive hand selection technique, in which a visible virtual hand acts as an avatar of the user's physical hand and is tied to it through a one-to-one mapping of the physical hand's motion and orientation, typically implemented with three-dimensional (3D) tracked controllers, allowing natural hand movements.

never_defined.name: hand velocity
never_defined.definition: The prism technique is an improvement of the go-go technique that applies scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's physical hand moves below a specified speed, and if the hand velocity is slower than a specified minimum velocity, the virtual hand remains still.

never_defined.name: travel technique
